title: Gospel of Thomas, sayings 65-71 (Nag Hammadi Codex II, page 45)
source: Nag Hammadi Codex II page photographs (Claremont Colleges Digital Library, Nag Hammadi Archive) + Coptic SCRIPTORIUM edition by Paul Dilley (CC BY 4.0) + English by Mark M. Mattison (public domain)
description: Gospel of Thomas, sayings 65-71, in the Coptic of Nag Hammadi Codex II, page 45, with each saying linked to the photograph of the papyrus page and an English translation.
introduction:
The Gospel of Thomas is a collection of 114 sayings attributed to Jesus, introduced as the hidden sayings written down by Didymos Judas Thomas. The only complete copy is the second tractate of Nag Hammadi Codex II, a papyrus book in Coptic copied in the 4th century and found near Nag Hammadi in Upper Egypt in 1945; it is now in the Coptic Museum, Cairo (inv. 10544). Greek fragments of the work survive in three Oxyrhynchus papyri (P. Oxy. 1, 654 and 655), which are not shown here.

This entry covers the sayings 65-71, which begin on codex page 45. The Coptic is given line by line; the small numbers are codex page and line (for example 33.5), so each line can be found on the photograph. Page and line breaks follow the Coptic SCRIPTORIUM edition by Paul Dilley, which he made from the photographs of The Facsimile Edition of the Nag Hammadi Codices, the negatives shown here.

Photograph: Codex II page 45, A-Series negative by Basile Psiroukis, Facsimile Edition p. 55, CCDL nha 2822; Nag Hammadi Archive of the Institute for Antiquity and Christianity, Claremont Colleges Digital Library. Checked on the photograph: page 45 line 1 begins 'ⲡⲉϫⲁϥ ϫⲉⲟⲩⲣⲱⲙⲉ ⲛⲭⲣ̣ⲏ̣[ⲥⲧⲟ]ⲥ̣ ⲛⲉⲩⲛ[ⲧⲁϥ]' and line 35 reads 'ⲁⲩⲱ ⲙⲛ̄ⲗⲁⲁⲩ ⲛⲁϣⲕⲟⲧϥ . [........]' (the lower lines break off at a hole on the right).
translator_notes: Coptic: Coptic SCRIPTORIUM edition (Paul C. Dilley), version 6.2.0, CC BY 4.0, shown in the manuscript's own spelling with words grouped as bound groups. Editorial signs are the edition's: square brackets mark letters lost in a gap (restored by the editor, or dots for the number of lost letters), a dot under a letter marks an uncertain reading, round brackets write out a letter abbreviated by a stroke at a line end, angle brackets mark letters added by the editor, curly brackets letters the editor removes, double square brackets letters erased by the scribe.

The small numbers in the Coptic are codex page and line (page.line) as marked in the edition. Where a word is divided between two lines on the papyrus, the edition sometimes keeps the word whole on one line, so a line can begin a few letters earlier or later on the photograph (for example 39.33-34, and the page change inside saying 13).

English: Mark M. Mattison, The Gospel of Thomas (public domain). Mattison's symbols: [ ] gap in the text, ( ) editorial insertion, / \ editorial correction of a scribal error. The saying headings are his.
Saying 65: Mattison's 'creditor' fills a gap in the papyrus; 'a good person' has also been proposed (M. W. Grondin).

translation.text:
He said, "A [creditor] owned a vineyard. He leased it out to some sharecroppers to work it so he could collect its fruit.

"He sent his servant so that the sharecroppers could give him the fruit of the vineyard. They seized his servant, beat him, and nearly killed him.

"The servant went back and told his master. His master said, 'Maybe he just didn't know them.' He sent another servant, but the tenants beat that one too.

"Then the master sent his son, thinking, 'Maybe they'll show some respect to my son.'

"Because they knew that he was the heir of the vineyard, the sharecroppers seized and killed him. Anyone who has ears to hear should hear!"
